title: Uzbekistan and the Silk Road: A Ten-Day Itinerary
metaDescription: A complete Uzbekistan itinerary covering Tashkent, Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva — transport, costs, when to go and what to expect.
excerpt: Turquoise domes, desert cities and high-speed trains between them. Central Asia has become one of the easiest great journeys to make.
author: Travel Editors
content:
For most of the last century, the Silk Road cities were effectively unreachable — closed borders, difficult visas, minimal infrastructure. Then Uzbekistan removed visa requirements for dozens of nationalities, built a high-speed rail network between its major cities, and became, almost overnight, one of the most accessible great journeys in the world.

Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva are not ruins. They are functioning cities with monumental Islamic architecture at a scale that is difficult to prepare for — tiled domes, vast madrasas, minarets that have been standing for eight hundred years.

## When to Go

Uzbekistan has a continental desert climate, which means the shoulder seasons are not optional.

- **April to early June** — the best window. Warm, clear, green after the spring rain
- **September to early November** — equally good, with melon season in September
- **July and August** — genuinely dangerous heat, regularly above 40°C. Sightseeing is limited to early morning and evening
- **December to February** — cold, occasionally below freezing, and atmospheric. Very few visitors and low prices

![Uzbekistan travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1525260268417-e73c4edc9d74?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## The Route

**Tashkent — 1 to 2 days**

The capital, largely rebuilt after a 1966 earthquake, which makes it more Soviet-modernist than ancient. The metro is the attraction people do not expect: ornate, marble-clad stations that were a state secret and forbidden to photograph until recently. Add the Chorsu Bazaar, the Khast Imam complex and a good museum or two.

Most trips start here because it is where the international flights land.

**Samarkand — 2 to 3 days**

The one everybody has heard of, and it justifies the reputation.

- **Registan** — three madrasas facing a single square, covered in blue and gold tilework. Go twice: once in daylight and once after dark when it is lit
- **Shah-i-Zinda** — a narrow avenue of mausoleums with the most intense tilework in the country. Go at opening time
- **Gur-e-Amir** — Timur's tomb, compact and extraordinary
- **Bibi-Khanym Mosque** — enormous, partly ruined, humbling
- **Siab Bazaar** — where the city actually shops

Samarkand has been heavily restored, and some of the restoration is more enthusiastic than archaeological. It remains one of the most visually overwhelming places in Asia.

**Bukhara — 2 to 3 days**

If Samarkand is monumental, Bukhara is **atmospheric**. The historic centre is largely intact rather than restored, and you can walk it for days.

- **Poi Kalyan** — the minaret Genghis Khan reportedly spared, alongside the mosque and madrasa
- **Lyabi-Hauz** — a plaza around an old pool, shaded by mulberry trees, where the city gathers in the evening
- **The Ark** — the emir's fortress
- **Chor Minor** — a small four-towered gatehouse, oddly charming
- **The trading domes** — covered bazaars still in use

Bukhara is the town most people say they would return to. Stay inside the old town in a converted merchant's house.

**Khiva — 1 to 2 days**

A walled desert city, almost entirely preserved, which feels like a film set and was very nearly abandoned before restoration. The whole of **Itchan Kala** — the inner walled town — is a museum, and staying inside the walls means having it to yourself after the day-trippers leave. Climb the watchtower at sunset.

Khiva is the furthest from Tashkent and the one most often cut for time. Try not to cut it.

![Uzbekistan travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1554058922-d51b58b707f5?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Getting Around

This is the part that has transformed.

**The Afrosiyob high-speed train** connects Tashkent, Samarkand and Bukhara quickly, comfortably and cheaply. Tashkent to Samarkand takes roughly two hours. **Book several days ahead** — these sell out, particularly in shoulder season.

**Khiva** is further. Options are an overnight train from Bukhara, a domestic flight to nearby Urgench, or a long desert drive. The overnight train is the classic choice and perfectly comfortable.

**Within cities**, taxis are inexpensive and ride-hailing apps work in Tashkent. Shared taxis handle intercity routes where trains do not.

## What It Costs

Excellent value:

- **Budget** — $30–45 per day
- **Mid-range** — $60–100
- **Comfortable** — $140–220

Boutique guesthouses in restored merchant houses in Bukhara and Khiva are one of the best accommodation propositions anywhere at the price.

## Practicalities

- **Visas** — visa-free for a long list of nationalities including most of Europe, and an e-visa for others. Check your own status; the list has expanded repeatedly
- **Currency** — the som. ATMs are reliable in cities, scarcer elsewhere. Carry cash for bazaars and taxis
- **Language** — Uzbek and Russian. English is growing in tourism but not widespread. A translation app earns its place here
- **Dress** — Uzbekistan is secular and relaxed, but modest dress is appreciated at religious sites. Women do not generally need a headscarf except in active mosques
- **Alcohol** — available and unremarkable
- **Food** — plov (the national rice dish, regionally variable and taken seriously), samsa, shashlik, lagman noodles, non bread, and extraordinary melons in season. Vegetarians should plan ahead; meat is central

## A Ten-Day Itinerary

- **Days 1–2** — Tashkent
- **Day 3** — train to Samarkand
- **Days 4–5** — Samarkand
- **Day 6** — train to Bukhara
- **Days 7–8** — Bukhara
- **Day 9** — overnight train or flight to Khiva
- **Day 10** — Khiva, then return

With fourteen days, add the **Nurata mountains and a yurt camp** at Aydarkul Lake between Samarkand and Bukhara, or the **Fergana Valley** for silk and ceramics.

## What to Expect

Uzbekistan is safe, hospitable and genuinely curious about visitors. Expect to be invited to sit, to be given tea, and to be photographed by school groups.

It is also still building its tourism infrastructure. Service can be uneven, English limited, and some restoration is heavy-handed. The compensation is that you are looking at architecture on a scale that Europe simply does not have, in cities that were the intellectual centre of the world while London was a market town — and you are usually looking at it without a queue.

The train bookings are the one thing that genuinely constrains this trip, so settle the route and the dates before anything else. Mapping the four cities and the train legs into a shared plan on **Trypinn** makes the sequencing obvious, and makes it clear which nights are fixed by a train ticket and which are yours.
